name: Vibrant Green
lede: Vibrant Green is a descriptive name for a pure, saturated green; painters long sought strong greens, and verdigris was the best they had until the 1800s.

sections.title: A modifier, not a shade
sections.body: The name is a plain modifier plus a basic color word, not a coined shade [1]. The library traces the color to three sources: ISCC-NBS block 130 (1955), RAL 6037 (1927) and the xkcd color survey (2010) [1]. The screen value is an approximation of a printed standard [1]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[vibrant-green]], [[lime-green]] and [[malachite]]; all are within about five units [2].

sections.title: Vibrant greens before screens
sections.body: Coles names verdigris as the most vibrant green available to them until then [3]. It was unstable, and turned from green to dark brown beside sulphur-bearing pigments such as ultramarine or orpiment [3]. A medieval alternative was saffron yellow combined with azurite, which Ball describes as giving a vibrant green [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering at least 1% of its canvas, within a distance of 4 units, as photographed [5]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and photographs of varnished paintings are not pigment tests.
